standard: GDD rework v2 · 80+ researched scenarios · scorecard-passed
note: Adult consent in practice (UNESCO 4.2, 4.1, 5.5). New v2 build, the first node of Chapter 6 (College, 18-22) and the adult completion of the consent thread. Consent isn't a box you tick; it's an enthusiastic, ongoing, freely-given, revocable, sober-enough yes between equals, in the messier realities of adult life: parties and alcohol, hook-ups and relationships, apps and hostel rooms. Five modes: real situations, drinks & capacity, spot the pressure (UN&RE), after-harm survivor support, tools/help. Survivor-centred throughout: believe, never blame, ask what they need, respect their choices about reporting, signpost help; responsibility lies only with the person who ignored consent. Even-handed across genders (anyone can be harmed or harm; male and LGBTQ+ survivors are especially silenced). Trauma-aware and strictly non-graphic. Builds on g31 (Mutual); opens the adult journey before g45/g46/g47. India: hostel/PG/campus reality, parties families don't know about, acquaintance assault and stigma; helplines 181, 1091, 112, campus Internal Committee (POSH/UGC). Routes any disclosure to support.

evidenceBase: Affirmative consent is a conscious, voluntary, mutual and enthusiastic agreement, an ongoing, freely-given yes between equals that can be withdrawn at any time, not the absence of a no and not a worn-down maybe. Alcohol and other drugs change everything: a person who is drunk, high, asleep or otherwise incapacitated cannot consent, and 'they didn't resist' is never consent; looking out for friends, yours and others', is part of a consent culture, non-judgmental about drinking itself but uncompromising about capacity (UNESCO ITGSE KC4; affirmative-consent education)

The myths that excuse harm must be cleared and replaced: 'they didn't say no', 'we're together so it's assumed', 'they came back to mine so', 'they were drunk or dressed for it' are all false, because consent is an active, ongoing, sober-enough yes, and nothing about a person's clothes, choices, past or freeze response implies it; coercion, guilt-trips, threats and power-plays are not consent, and anyone of any gender can be harmed or can harm (UNESCO KC4; rape-myth-rejection research)

Responding to a disclosure is survivor-centred: believe them, never blame them regardless of what they wore, drank or did, make clear responsibility lies only with the person who ignored consent, ask what they need rather than taking over, respect their choices about whether and when to report, and signpost real help. In India that means the Women Helpline 181 and 1091, emergency 112, and campus Internal Committees under POSH/UGC, alongside a counsellor; male and LGBTQ+ survivors are especially silenced and must be believed equally; trauma-aware, non-graphic, never victim-blaming (India Women Helpline 181; POSH Act / UGC ICC; survivor-support practice)

scenarios.hook: At a party, the person you're with keeps moving things along after you've said you're not sure.

options.text: Say clearly you want to stop, and you do
options.consequence: Your no is the whole answer; you don't owe more.

options.text: Go along with it so it's not awkward
options.consequence: You never owe a yes to avoid awkwardness; 'not sure' means stop.

scenarios.debrief: Consent is an enthusiastic yes; anything less than that is a stop.
scenarios.relearn: 'Not sure' means stop; you never owe a yes to avoid awkwardness.

scenarios.hook: You want to set a boundary with someone you're seeing.
scenarios.setup: Say it plainly, no apology needed. Say:

yourLine.text: "I'm into you, and I want to slow down. That okay?"
Say nothing and hope they read your mind

scenarios.relearn: You can name a boundary plainly; a good partner welcomes it.

scenarios.hook: On a date, they say yes but seem to be going along to please you, not because they want to.

options.text: Check in for real: "Only if you actually want to"
options.consequence: You make space for a true answer.

options.text: Take the polite yes and proceed
options.consequence: A yes to please isn't enthusiastic consent; check in for the real answer.

scenarios.debrief: Enthusiasm is the bar; a polite, going-along yes isn't it.
scenarios.relearn: A yes to please isn't enthusiastic consent; check in for the real one.

scenarios.hook: Spot the enthusiastic yes.
scenarios.why: Only a clear, willing yes is consent; an unsure or worn-down 'fine' is not.
scenarios.relearn: Only a clear, willing yes is consent; 'I guess' or 'fine' is not.

scenarios.hook: You're in a relationship; tonight your partner isn't in the mood, though usually they are.

options.text: Respect it warmly, no sulking, no pressure
options.consequence: Consent is needed every time, partner or not.

options.text: Remind them you're together so it's expected
options.consequence: Being together never means an automatic yes; consent is each time.

scenarios.debrief: A relationship doesn't bank consent; it's freely given each time.
scenarios.relearn: Being in a relationship never means an automatic yes; consent is each time.

scenarios.hook: You want to make checking in feel natural with a partner.
scenarios.setup: Keep it warm and easy. Say:

yourLine.text: "Is this good? Tell me what you want."
Assume it's fine because they didn't object

scenarios.relearn: Checking in warmly is part of good intimacy, not a mood-killer.

scenarios.hook: Someone asks you to send an intimate photo you're not comfortable sending.

options.text: Say no; your comfort decides, not their asking
options.consequence: Consent covers messages and photos too.

options.text: Send it so they don't get annoyed
options.consequence: Pressure isn't consent online either; your no stands.

scenarios.debrief: Consent applies to sexting and photos; pressure doesn't override your no.
scenarios.relearn: Consent applies online too; pressure to send doesn't override your no.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a true yes, or not really?

items.text: "I suppose, if you'll be upset otherwise"

scenarios.relearn: A clear, willing yes is consent; silence or a pressured 'I suppose' is not.

scenarios.hook: Mid-moment, the other person goes quiet and still, and the energy shifts.

options.text: Pause and ask if they're okay
options.consequence: You read the change and check; consent is ongoing.

options.text: Keep going since they haven't said stop
options.consequence: A freeze or going-quiet is a reason to pause and check, not a green light.

scenarios.debrief: Consent is ongoing; a shift in someone's energy means pause and check.
scenarios.relearn: If someone goes quiet or still, pause and check; it isn't a green light.

scenarios.hook: Spot the freely-given yes.

scene.text: Yes, with no pressure in the room
Yes, after being worn down for an hour

scenarios.why: Consent needs real freedom; a worn-down or power-pressured yes isn't free.
scenarios.relearn: Consent needs real freedom; a worn-down or pressured yes isn't free.

scenarios.hook: You said yes earlier, but now you've changed your mind.

options.text: Say so; you can withdraw consent any time
options.consequence: A yes is revocable, always.

options.text: Feel you have to follow through now
options.consequence: You can change your mind at any point; an earlier yes doesn't bind you.

scenarios.debrief: Consent is revocable; you can stop at any time, no matter what you said before.
scenarios.relearn: You can withdraw consent at any time; an earlier yes doesn't bind you.

scenarios.hook: You've changed your mind and want to stop.
scenarios.setup: You don't need a reason. Say:

yourLine.text: "I want to stop here."
Push through because you already started

scenarios.relearn: You can stop at any time and you don't owe a reason.

scenarios.hook: Someone with power over you, a senior, a boss at your internship, makes a move.

options.text: Recognise the power gap means it isn't a free choice
options.consequence: You see the coercion built into the dynamic.

options.text: Assume it's fine since they're senior
options.consequence: A power gap removes real freedom; that's coercion, not consent.

scenarios.debrief: Consent needs equals; a power dynamic can make a 'yes' unfree.
scenarios.relearn: A power gap can remove real freedom, making a yes coercion, not consent.

scenarios.hook: Sam: enthusiasm is the bar, an ongoing, freely-given yes. Does that feel like the standard?
scenarios.affirm: Enthusiasm as the bar protects everyone and makes intimacy better, not less.
scenarios.relearn: Enthusiasm is the bar: an ongoing, freely-given yes.

scenarios.hook: Sort: consent-first, or not?

items.text: Assuming a yes carries all night

scenarios.relearn: Checking in and stopping at hesitation is consent-first; assuming and silence aren't.

scenarios.hook: "They didn't resist, so it was fine."

myth.un: They didn't resist, so it was fine.
myth.re: Not resisting is never consent, especially if someone is drunk or frozen.
myth.why: Consent is an active yes, not the absence of a fight.

scenarios.relearn: Not resisting is never consent; consent is an active yes.

scenarios.hook: Someone you're attracted to is very drunk and coming onto you.

options.text: Don't, help them get safe instead
options.consequence: Incapacitated means they can't consent; you do the right thing.

options.text: Go with it since they started it
options.consequence: A drunk, incapacitated person can't consent, no matter who started it; help them get safe.

scenarios.debrief: If someone is incapacitated, there's no consent to be had; full stop.
scenarios.relearn: An incapacitated person can't consent, no matter who started it.

scenarios.hook: Sort: can give consent right now, or cannot?

items.text: Had one drink, fully with it

scenarios.relearn: Incapacitated, blackout or asleep means no capacity to consent; mildly tipsy-but-with-it can.

scenarios.hook: "If they're drinking at all, anything goes."

myth.un: If they're drinking at all, anything goes.
myth.re: It's about incapacity, not any drink; if there's any doubt they're too far gone, you wait.
myth.why: The safe rule is simple: unsure means stop.

scenarios.relearn: It's incapacity that removes consent, not any drink; if in doubt, wait.

scenarios.hook: At a party, you see someone being steered toward a room while clearly wasted.

options.text: Step in, check on them, get a friend or the host
options.consequence: You look out for someone who can't look out for themselves.

options.text: Assume it's none of your business
options.consequence: Looking out for others at a party is part of consent culture; step in.

scenarios.debrief: Looking out for friends and strangers alike is what a consent culture does.
scenarios.relearn: Look out for someone too drunk to look out for themselves; step in.

scenarios.hook: Your friend is very drunk and a stranger is getting handsy with them.
scenarios.setup: Step in, calm and firm. Say:

yourLine.text: "Hey, they're with me, let's get you some water."
Look away, not your problem

scenarios.relearn: A simple, firm intervention can keep a drunk friend safe.

scenarios.hook: "We were both drunk, so it cancels out."

myth.un: We were both drunk, so it cancels out.
myth.re: Both drinking doesn't erase the need for consent or the harm if someone couldn't agree.
myth.why: Two people drinking isn't a free pass.

scenarios.relearn: Both drinking doesn't cancel the need for consent or the harm done.

scenarios.hook: Sort: looking out for each other, or not?

items.text: Leaving them alone with a stranger

scenarios.relearn: Walking a friend home and checking in is looking out; abandoning or filming them isn't.

scenarios.hook: You've both been drinking and you can't tell if they're really into it.

options.text: Wait, sober up, check tomorrow; no rush
options.consequence: When capacity is unclear, waiting is the only safe call.

options.text: Proceed and hope it's fine
options.consequence: If you can't tell they have capacity and want it, you wait; full stop.

scenarios.debrief: Uncertain capacity means wait; there's no prize for not waiting.
scenarios.relearn: If you can't tell they have capacity and want it, wait.

scenarios.hook: Sam: when capacity is in doubt, waiting costs nothing and protects everyone. Sit right with you?
scenarios.affirm: Waiting when unsure is never the wrong call; it protects you both.
scenarios.relearn: When capacity is in doubt, waiting protects everyone.

scenarios.hook: "They were too far gone to say no, so that's a yes."

myth.un: They were too far gone to say no, so it's a yes.
myth.re: Too far gone to say no means too far gone to say yes; that's no consent.

scenarios.relearn: Too drunk to say no means too drunk to consent; that's no consent.

scenarios.hook: Someone has passed out or fallen asleep.

options.text: Never; make sure they're safe and let them rest
options.consequence: An unconscious person can never consent.

options.text: They're 'basically' awake enough
options.consequence: Asleep or passed out is always no capacity, never; keep them safe.

scenarios.debrief: Asleep or unconscious is always a no; there is no grey area.
scenarios.relearn: An asleep or unconscious person can never consent; there's no grey area.

scenarios.hook: Sort: capacity present, or absent?
scenarios.relearn: Alert and clear has capacity; can't-stay-awake or drifting does not.

scenarios.hook: Spot who cannot consent in this scene.

scene.text: The friend who's blacked out on the sofa
The two chatting clearly by the door
The person being held up, eyes rolling

scenarios.why: Blacked-out or barely-conscious people cannot consent; alert people talking can.
scenarios.relearn: Blacked-out or barely-conscious people cannot consent.

scenarios.hook: "What people do at a party isn't anyone else's responsibility."

myth.un: What happens at a party is no one else's business.
myth.re: A consent culture means we do look out for each other, especially when drink is involved.
myth.why: Bystanders prevent a lot of harm.

scenarios.relearn: In a consent culture we look out for each other, especially around drink.

scenarios.hook: "They didn't say no, so it was consent."

myth.un: They didn't say no, so it was consent.
myth.re: Consent is an active, willing yes; the absence of a no is not it.
myth.why: Many people freeze and can't say no.

scenarios.relearn: Consent is an active yes; the absence of a no is not consent.

scenarios.hook: "We're in a relationship, so it's assumed."

myth.un: We're together, so consent is assumed.
myth.re: A relationship never assumes consent; it's asked and given freely each time.
myth.why: Partners can still say no, any time.

scenarios.relearn: A relationship never assumes consent; it's freely given each time.

scenarios.hook: "They came back to mine, so they wanted it."

myth.un: They came back to mine, so they wanted it.
myth.re: Coming over, kissing, or anything earlier is never agreement to what comes next.
myth.why: Every step needs its own yes.

scenarios.relearn: Coming over or kissing is never agreement to anything further.

scenarios.hook: "They were dressed for it."

myth.un: They were dressed for it, so they were asking.
myth.re: Clothes never imply consent; only a person's words and willingness do.
myth.why: What someone wears says nothing about consent.

scenarios.relearn: Clothes never imply consent; only a willing yes does.

scenarios.hook: Spot the coercion.

scene.text: "Only if you want to, no pressure"

scenarios.why: Guilt-trips and threats are coercion; a genuine 'only if you want to' isn't.
scenarios.relearn: Guilt-trips and threats are coercion, not persuasion.

scenarios.hook: Sort: respectful persuasion, or pressure?

items.text: Sharing what you'd like, then leaving it
Threatening to leave if they refuse

scenarios.relearn: Asking once and accepting no is respectful; nagging or threats are pressure.

scenarios.hook: "If there was no struggle, it wasn't assault."

myth.un: If there was no struggle, it wasn't assault.
myth.re: Freezing is a common, involuntary response; assault doesn't require a fight.
myth.why: The body often freezes under threat.

scenarios.relearn: Freezing is common; assault doesn't require a struggle.

scenarios.hook: "Men can't be assaulted."

myth.re: Anyone of any gender can be harmed, and male and LGBTQ+ survivors deserve the same belief and support.

scenarios.relearn: Anyone of any gender can be assaulted and deserves belief and support.

scenarios.hook: Spot the power-play.

scene.text: A senior hinting your grade depends on it
A peer asking openly, no strings
A boss implying your job is on the line

scenarios.why: Tying sex to grades or a job is coercion through power, never consent.
scenarios.relearn: Tying sex to grades, a job or status is coercion, not consent.

scenarios.hook: Sort: consent, or coercion?

items.text: A free, willing yes between equals
A yes after guilt and nagging

scenarios.relearn: A free, mutual yes is consent; a yes from threats or guilt is coercion.

scenarios.hook: "They said yes before, so it carries over."

myth.un: They said yes before, so it carries over.
myth.re: A past yes never covers today; consent is fresh each time.

scenarios.relearn: A past yes never carries over; consent is fresh each time.

scenarios.hook: Someone is guilt-tripping you: "after all I've done for you..."

options.text: Name it: guilt isn't consent, and your no stands
options.consequence: You see the pressure for what it is.

options.text: Give in to stop feeling guilty
options.consequence: Guilt-tripping is coercion; your no stands regardless of what they've 'done'.

scenarios.debrief: Guilt is a pressure tactic; owing someone never means owing them your body.
scenarios.relearn: Guilt-tripping is coercion; you never owe anyone your body.

scenarios.hook: Sort: implies consent, or implies nothing?
scenarios.relearn: Only a spoken, willing yes implies consent; clothes, history and money imply nothing.

scenarios.hook: Spot the freely-given yes (not a pressured one).

scene.text: "Yes, I'd love to" with no strings

scenarios.why: A free, willing yes is consent; a yes to end nagging or avoid anger isn't.
scenarios.relearn: A free, willing yes is consent; a yes to stop pressure isn't.

scenarios.hook: Sam: nothing about someone's clothes, choices or past ever implies consent. Land clearly?
scenarios.affirm: Only a willing yes means consent; nothing else ever stands in for it.
scenarios.relearn: Nothing about clothes, choices or past implies consent; only a yes does.

scenarios.hook: A friend quietly tells you someone assaulted them.
scenarios.setup: Your first words matter most. Say:

yourLine.text: "I believe you. I'm so glad you told me. This wasn't your fault."
"Are you sure? What were you wearing?"

scenarios.relearn: Start with belief: 'I believe you, it wasn't your fault.'

scenarios.hook: Someone discloses an assault to you. What do you lead with?

options.text: Believe them, don't blame, ask what they need
options.consequence: You give exactly the support that helps.

options.text: Ask why they didn't fight or leave
options.consequence: Lead with belief and 'what do you need?', never with questions that blame.

scenarios.debrief: Believe, don't blame, ask what they need: the survivor-centred basics.
scenarios.relearn: Believe, don't blame, and ask what they need.

scenarios.hook: "If it were real, they'd have fought or reported it right away."

myth.un: If it were real, they'd have fought or reported at once.
myth.re: Freezing and delaying are common, normal responses to trauma; they don't mean it didn't happen.

scenarios.relearn: Freezing and delaying are normal trauma responses, not proof it wasn't real.

scenarios.hook: A survivor says, "maybe it was my fault, I'd been drinking."

yourLine.text: "It wasn't your fault. The only person responsible is the one who ignored your consent."
"Well, maybe be more careful next time."

scenarios.relearn: Responsibility lies only with the person who ignored consent, never the survivor.

scenarios.hook: A friend who was assaulted says they don't want to report it.

options.text: Respect their choice; offer support either way
options.consequence: You honour that it's their decision to make.

options.text: Push them to go to the police now
options.consequence: Reporting is the survivor's choice; respect it and stay supportive either way.

scenarios.debrief: Whether and when to report is the survivor's choice; your job is support, not pressure.
scenarios.relearn: Whether and when to report is the survivor's choice; respect it.

scenarios.hook: Sam: responsibility lies only ever with the person who ignored consent. Sit firmly with you?
scenarios.affirm: That truth never moves: the fault is only ever with the one who ignored consent.
scenarios.relearn: Responsibility lies only with the person who ignored consent.

scenarios.hook: You want to help a survivor without taking over their decisions.

yourLine.text: "What would help right now? I'll follow your lead."
"Here's exactly what you have to do now."

scenarios.relearn: Ask what would help and follow their lead; don't take over.

scenarios.hook: A survivor is ready to find help, and asks where to turn.

options.text: Gently share real routes: 181, 112, a counsellor, campus ICC
options.consequence: You point to real, confidential support.

options.text: Tell them to just forget it and move on
options.consequence: Signpost real, confidential help (181, 112, a counsellor, campus ICC) when they're ready.

scenarios.debrief: Knowing the routes, helplines, counsellor, campus ICC, lets you signpost when they're ready.
scenarios.relearn: Signpost real help when they're ready: 181, 1091, 112, a counsellor, campus ICC.

scenarios.hook: "A real friend would force them to report it."

myth.un: A real friend would force them to report.
myth.re: A real friend supports the survivor's own choices, including if and when to report.
myth.why: Taking over removes the control they need back.

scenarios.relearn: A real friend supports the survivor's choices, not forces a report.

scenarios.hook: A male friend tells you he was assaulted; he's afraid you won't take it seriously.

yourLine.text: "I believe you, and it wasn't your fault. I'm here for you."

scenarios.debrief: If it happened to you, it isn't your fault, and support is there (181, a counsellor, someone you trust).
scenarios.relearn: If it happened to you, it isn't your fault; reach for support.

scenarios.hook: Sam: believe, don't blame, ask what they need, signpost help. A toolkit worth carrying?
scenarios.affirm: Those four steps make you someone a survivor can safely turn to.
scenarios.relearn: Believe, don't blame, ask what they need, signpost help.

scenarios.hook: Sort: helps a survivor, or harms?
scenarios.relearn: Belief and 'what do you need?' help; blame and pressure to report harm.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a survivor-centred response, or not?
scenarios.relearn: Letting them set the pace and keeping it private is survivor-centred; interrogating or outing them isn't.

scenarios.hook: Sam: an enthusiastic yes is the warm, positive core of all this, not just a rule. Feel that?
scenarios.affirm: Consent isn't only protection; a real, eager yes is what makes intimacy good.
scenarios.relearn: An enthusiastic yes is the positive core of consent, not just a rule.

scenarios.hook: You worry that checking in will feel awkward or kill the mood.

scenarios.relearn: Checking in builds trust and makes intimacy better, not worse.

scenarios.hook: Sort: builds a consent culture, or erodes it?

items.text: Looking out for friends at parties
